transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. Can you tell me what brings you in today?

Oh, hello Doctor. Thank you so much for seeing me today, I hope I'm not taking up too much of your time. I... well, my family thought it would be best if I came in. 

It's just... we've had a terrible shock. My grandson was killed recently, and I've been trying so hard to be strong for everyone, I really have. But I came in because... well, I feel so awful even saying this out loud. Please don't think I'm a terrible mother. It's just... my daughter, she's so sweet, she'll sit right beside me and hold my hand, and I know I love her, I really do. But... I cannot feel the warmth of it inside me at all right now. 

I just can't feel it. Does that make sense, Doctor? Am I explaining that right?
How long have you been feeling this way emotionally since your grandson's passing?

Well, I suppose it's... it's been six days now. Yes, six days since... since it happened. Outside the community center. 

I hope I'm not making too much of a fuss over just a few days. I know it hasn't been that long, and I really should be pulling myself together better by now, shouldn't I? I just... I don't want to be a burden on them when they're already hurting so much. Is it normal to feel this numb after less than a week, Doctor? I just want to make sure I'm not doing something wrong.
Have you been having trouble sleeping since your grandson passed away?

Oh, no, Doctor. I... well, to be completely honest, I haven't had any trouble at all with my sleep. I just go to bed and close my eyes and... I sleep right through until morning. 

I actually feel quite dreadful admitting that. My poor daughter is up half the night crying, and I'm just asleep. I hope you don't think less of me for being able to rest when everything is in such a terrible state. I suppose my old body is just... shutting down from the exhaustion of it all? I hope that's an alright way to react. It doesn't mean I don't care, does it?
Have you found that you don't take pleasure in things you usually enjoy, like hobbies, spending time with family, or other activities?

Well, I... I suppose I've still been doing my usual things. I mean, I try to keep busy, you know? It's important to keep the house tidy and make sure everyone has something to eat. 

I wouldn't say I've stopped enjoying things, exactly. I still go to my Thursday morning knitting group, and... and I smile and nod when the ladies tell their stories. I hope that's the right thing to do. I don't want to bring the mood down or make anyone uncomfortable. 

I guess I'm just... going through the motions a bit? But I'm still participating, I really am. I haven't just given up on everything. That's a good sign, isn't it, Doctor? That I'm still trying to keep up with my little routines?
Doctor: Have you felt down or depressed most of the day, nearly every day, since your grandson passed away?

Oh, no, Doctor, I wouldn't say depressed. I... well, I try very hard to keep my chin up. It wouldn't do anyone any good if I just sat around moping all day, would it? 

I mean, I'm terribly sad about my grandson, of course I am, but I make sure to get up and put my clothes on and just... keep going. I really try to be strong for my daughter and the rest of the family. I hope that's the right way to handle things. You don't think I'm being cold or unfeeling by not crying all day, do you? I just want to be helpful and not make things worse for them by falling apart. That's the best thing I can do right now, isn't it?
Have you noticed any change in how much you look forward to or enjoy your usual activities, like your knitting group or time with family?

Well, I... I suppose I still go to the knitting group, like I said, and I sit with my family. I try very hard to be present. But... 

Actually, Doctor, this is the main reason I came to see you. I feel so terrible admitting this, I really do. It's just... since my grandson was killed... my daughter can come and sit right beside me, and she'll hold my hand, and... in my head, I know I love her. I know she's my daughter and I love her dearly. But I just... I cannot feel the warmth of it inside me at all. 

It's like there's this awful emptiness where the love and the joy used to be. I smile at her, and I squeeze her hand back, because I want to be a good mother and comfort her, but I don't feel it. I feel so ashamed, Doctor. A mother should always feel love for her child, shouldn't she? I'm not a bad person for feeling this way, am I? I just want to be able to feel that warmth again so I can be there for her properly.
Doctor: Aside from the sadness related to your grandson’s passing, have you found yourself feeling down or emotionally low even when you’re not thinking about what happened?

Well, I... I don't think so, Doctor. I really try my best not to let myself get too low, you know? 

I mean, there's the terrible sadness about my grandson, of course, but I don't just sit around feeling miserable about everything else. I try to keep a positive outlook for the rest of the family. I think it's so important to keep your chin up and not become a burden to others. 

So, no, I wouldn't say I feel down when I'm not thinking about... about what happened. I just try to focus on what needs doing around the house. That's a healthy way to cope, isn't it? Just keeping busy and not dwelling on things too much? I really do want to make sure I'm handling all this the right way.
Have you noticed yourself participating less in activities you used to enjoy, even if you still go through the motions?

Well, I... I suppose I have stepped back just a little bit from a few things. I try so hard to keep up, because I always want to be useful, you know? But... oh, I feel dreadful even saying this out loud. 

I have stopped going to my walking club. I just haven't quite had it in me to keep pace with the other ladies lately. And... what makes me feel so much worse is that I just cannot bring myself to help with the funeral repast planning. 

I know I should be doing it. Those are the very people and duties my family depends on me for, usually. I'm always the one who organizes the food and makes sure everyone is taken care of. But I just can't seem to face it right now. I feel so incredibly selfish for stepping away from it. I'm not letting them down too terribly, am I, Doctor? I just hope it's alright that I need to step back from those duties just this once. It doesn't make me a bad grandmother, does it?

Doctor: When you attend your knitting group or spend time with your family, do you find that you’re just going through the motions without really feeling engaged or interested, even if you’re physically there?

Well, I... I suppose you could say that, yes. I do try so very hard to be present, like I said. I sit there with my knitting needles, and I smile, and I nod when the other ladies are talking. I really do try to be good company. 

But... oh, it's just like I mentioned before about my daughter. I'm there in the room, but my mind is just sort of... blank. I'm counting my stitches, but I couldn't tell you what the conversation was about five minutes later. I just feel so terribly rude, sitting there like a lump when they're all trying to be so nice to me. 

I'm still doing the right thing by going, though, aren't I? I don't want them to think I don't appreciate them, or that I'm just wallowing. It's better to go and just be quiet than to stay home and hide away, wouldn't you agree, Doctor? I just want to make sure I'm not being a bother to anyone by sitting there so quietly.

Doctor: When you're at your knitting group or going about your usual routines, do you find that you're not getting any pleasure from them anymore—even though you used to enjoy them before your grandson passed away?

Oh, no, Doctor... I wouldn't say that. I really do still enjoy my knitting, I promise. 

I know I said I get a bit distracted and quiet, but... well, seeing the beautiful yarn and watching a pattern come together, it still brings me a nice feeling. I'd hate for you to think I'm just sitting there completely miserable and ungrateful for my hobbies. I always try to find the good in things, even now. 

I think it's so important to hold onto those little joys and appreciate them, don't you? It shows I'm still trying my best to cope and be positive, right?

Doctor: Can you recall if you’ve felt any sense of enjoyment or satisfaction from your knitting or time with family since your grandson passed away, or does it all feel emotionally flat no matter what you’re doing?

Well, I... I suppose if I am being completely honest... oh, I hate to even admit this. It makes me sound so cold. 

I know I said I still enjoy my knitting, and I do try to focus on the pretty yarn. But... when it comes to the feelings inside, the real feelings... it's just so difficult right now. 

That's actually why I agreed to come see you today. Since my sweet grandson was killed... my daughter, she is just wonderful. She will come and sit right beside me, and she'll hold my hand. And in my head, I know I love her so very much. I know it. But... I just cannot feel the warmth of that love inside me at all. It's like there's a pane of glass between me and the feeling. 

I feel so terribly guilty about it. She's grieving too, and she's trying so hard to comfort me, and I just feel... empty. I'm not a bad mother for feeling that way, am I, Doctor? I'm sure it's just the shock, and it will pass if I just keep trying my best to be there for her, don't you think?
Since your grandson passed away, have you found it difficult to feel pleasure or joy in activities you used to enjoy, even when you're doing them?

Well, I... I know we just talked about this a little bit, and I really don't want to sound like a broken record, or like I'm just complaining... 

But yes, it's... it's like I was just saying about my daughter. That's the real reason I'm here. When she sits next to me and holds my hand... I know in my mind that I love her, but I just can't feel that warmth, that joy of being with her, inside me at all anymore. 

And it's the same with the knitting, or anything else that used to make me smile. I go through the motions, and I try so hard to be pleasant and appreciate things, but the good feelings just... they just aren't there right now. I hope you understand I'm not trying to be difficult or ungrateful, Doctor. I'm still trying my very best, aren't I?

Outside of your grief and interactions with your daughter, have you noticed that activities you used to enjoy — like your knitting or time with friends — feel less pleasurable than they used to, even when you're doing them?

Oh, dear... I feel terrible, I must not be answering your questions very well if you have to keep asking. I'm so sorry, Doctor, I really am trying to be helpful. 

I know I keep bringing it back to my daughter... it's just that not being able to feel that warmth when she holds my hand, like I mentioned, that was really the whole reason I finally agreed to come in and see you. It frightened me so much to feel so empty with my own child after losing my grandson. 

But to answer what you're asking about my friends and the knitting... yes, I suppose it's exactly the same there, too. I sit with the ladies, and they are so dear to me, and I know I should be having a lovely time. But I just feel so... blank inside. I don't let it show, of course. I'd never want to bring them down or seem ungrateful for their company. I just smile and keep my hands busy so they don't worry. That's the best way to handle it, don't you think? Just try to be pleasant and not be a burden to anyone?

Since your grandson passed away, have you found that activities you used to take joy in — like your knitting or time with your friends — no longer bring you the same sense of pleasure or satisfaction, even when you're doing them?

Oh, Doctor... I really am so sorry. I must be doing a terrible job explaining myself today. I know you've asked me about this a few times now, and I don't want you to think I'm ignoring your questions about the knitting or my friends. I'm really trying my best to answer you properly. 

It's just... the whole reason I'm sitting here in your office today is because of my daughter. When she comes over and sits right beside me, and she takes my hand... I know in my head that I love her. I do. But ever since my grandson was killed, I just cannot feel the warmth of that love inside me at all. Not even a little bit. 

That's the part that frightens me so much, and that's why I keep bringing it up. It makes me feel like such a terrible mother to not feel anything when she's trying so hard to comfort me. I suppose it's the same with the knitting and the ladies, like you said, but it's the feeling... or the lack of feeling... with my daughter that really pushed me to come see you. I hope you can forgive me for repeating myself, Doctor. I'm just so worried about being a burden to her, and I want to make sure I'm doing the right thing by being here. Am I making sense?
Have you noticed that you’ve lost interest in your usual activities — like knitting or seeing friends — even when you’re not thinking about your grandson?

Oh, goodness... no, I don't think I've lost interest. I still want to see my friends, and I still make sure to go to the knitting circle every week. I really do try to keep up with all my usual things, Doctor. 

I'd never want to just stop participating and make everyone worry about me, or have you think I'm just giving up. I know it's important to keep trying and to be a good friend. So I still have the interest to go and do those things, and I do go... it's just that blank feeling I get when I'm actually there, like we talked about. 

I haven't just lost interest and stopped caring, I promise. I hope that's a better answer for you? I really am trying to be as helpful as I can today.
Since your grandson passed away, have you found that nothing gives you pleasure like it used to — even the things you really enjoyed before, like knitting or spending time with friends?

Oh, my... I am so sorry, Doctor. I feel like we keep going over this, and it must be my fault for not making myself clear. I really don't want to frustrate you, I promise I'm trying my best. 

If you're asking if absolutely *nothing* gives me pleasure anymore... well, I certainly wouldn't say that. That sounds so terribly ungrateful, doesn't it? I still have so much to be thankful for, and I try very hard to count my blessings every single day. I wouldn't want you to think I'm just sitting around feeling sorry for myself or being entirely miserable. 

I still try to enjoy my life, I really do. I appreciate my friends so much, and I make sure to smile and be good company for them. It's just that blank feeling that sneaks up on me sometimes, like I mentioned before, but I promise I haven't let it ruin everything. I'm trying very hard to stay positive and not be a dark cloud. Does that make sense? I do hope I'm finally giving you the answers you need.
Can you describe how your enjoyment of knitting has changed since your grandson passed away, compared to how you used to feel before?

Oh, dear... I suppose I haven't really noticed a big change, not in the way you mean. I still pick up my needles every evening, just like I always have. I'm working on a lovely little cardigan right now, actually. 

I wouldn't want you to think I've just let my hobbies fall by the wayside. I know how important it is to keep one's hands busy, especially at my age. It's good for the mind, isn't it? So I still knit, and I still think the patterns are very pretty. I try very hard to appreciate the quiet time while I'm doing it. 

I don't think I could say my enjoyment has completely changed... I still do it, and I still try to be cheerful about it. I hope that's alright to say? I don't want to sound like I'm not paying attention to how I feel, I just... I try to focus on the good things, you know? I hope that answers what you were asking, Doctor.

When you're knitting or spending time with your friends, do you find that you're not feeling any real pleasure or satisfaction from them anymore, even though you used to before your grandson passed away?

Oh, I see... I'm so sorry, Doctor, I think I finally understand what you've been trying to ask me. I just... I didn't want to say it out loud because it makes me sound like such a dreadful, cold person. Please don't think badly of me, I really didn't want to disappoint you.

It’s just... well, since my grandson was killed, it's not just the knitting or the friends. It's... it's even with my own family. My daughter will come over and sit right beside me, and she'll hold my hand... and I know I love her, I know it in my head. But... I just cannot feel the warmth of it inside me at all. 

I feel so incredibly guilty even admitting that to you. I really am trying to feel that warmth again, I promise I am. I don't want you to think I'm a terrible mother for feeling so blank inside when she's trying to comfort me. Is... is that what you were asking about? I do hope I'm finally giving you the right answer.

Since your grandson passed away, have you noticed that even when you’re doing something you used to really enjoy — like knitting or being with friends — you don’t feel any real happiness or satisfaction from it at all?

Oh, my... I must not be explaining myself very well today, Doctor, and I am so sorry for making you ask me again. I really don't mean to be difficult or make you repeat yourself. 

But yes, it’s exactly like I was just trying to say... it's actually the main reason I finally agreed to come in and see you. Since my grandson was killed, it's like that with everything. Even when my own daughter sits right beside me and holds my hand. I know I love her, I really do, but I just cannot feel the warmth or the happiness of it inside me at all. And it's the same with my knitting and my friends. The joy just isn't there, no matter how hard I try to force it. 

I feel so dreadful saying it out loud again, it makes me sound so ungrateful. I really am trying to be better and appreciate these things, I promise you I am. Did I explain it properly this time? I just want to make sure I'm giving you the answers you need.
